description: Zero-G Health is a team of three students who met through the Hacking Health and Hacking Space hackathons. For the challenge “Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions”, we are building a tool that gathers health indicators and helps astronauts understand their condition and act on it, far from Earth.
summary:
Nobody notices a slow change. On a Mars mission the dangerous health effects are the slow ones, and the doctor is up to twenty minutes away, each way.

Baseline is health self-check software for astronauts. It learns each crew member's personal normal from a sensor headpiece they sleep in, asks for two minutes each morning, and flags slow drift weeks before a reading reaches a medical limit. Every flag comes with one plain next action and an escalation path: you, then the crew medical officer, then the flight surgeon. If an alarm goes unanswered, the watch calls the doctor on board.

We built a working web prototype that follows a simulated crew member through 180 days to Mars: a daily check, charts with a personal normal band, a clickable body map, a weekly report, and bone and muscle loss models based on NASA loss rates and standards. Every reading says how we know it, and we state plainly what the system cannot see.
details:
What it does

Baseline is a daily health self-check for astronauts on long missions. A headpiece with dry EEG, optical pulse (PPG), motion (IMU) and skin temperature sensors collects data during sleep and a two-minute morning check. The software learns each astronaut's own normal range, then compares every new reading to that personal band instead of a population limit. When a reading drifts outside the band, it is flagged long before it reaches the medical limit.

Hardware concept

The headgear is inspired by the Communications Carrier Assembly (CCA), the fabric "Snoopy cap" astronauts already wear under the helmet for communications. Our sensors are designed to be integrated into the lining of that cap, so the crew wears nothing new during launch, landing and spacewalks, and the voice reading reuses the cap's existing microphones. A soft headband version covers sleep and the daily morning check. This is a design concept: no hardware was built, and the prototype runs on simulated data.

How it works

- Three states only: in your normal, drifting, at limit. Status is shown by shape as well as colour.

- Every flag carries one plain next action and an escalation ladder: you, crew medical officer, flight surgeon. The watch can call the crew medical officer if an alarm is not answered.

- A clickable body map shows which sensor feeds which part of the body.

- Each reading is tagged with how we know it: sensed, estimated by ML, estimated by model, self-measured, or from the ship.

- A weekly report summarises the trends for the crew and the ground.

Bone and muscle loss

Bone density cannot be measured in flight, so we built two day-by-day models in C that estimate it from what the crew already logs. An activity module turns accelerometer data and the training log into an exercise dose. A nutrition module compares daily intake with NASA JSC-67378 requirements. The bone model starts from NASA's 1 to 1.5 % monthly loss rate and adjusts it for exercise and nutrition. The muscle model tracks legs, back, calves and upper body separately and runs 27 anomaly checks, including a weekly strength test that catches losses the model cannot see, such as an injury. The algorithms are in the Algorithms folder of our repository, and the web app runs the same models live.

Benefits and impact

With a communication delay of up to about 20 minutes each way, a Mars crew cannot rely on real-time medical support. Baseline gives each astronaut an early, personal warning and a clear action, and gives flight surgeons a short summary instead of raw data. Raw brain and voice signals stay on board.

Honesty

All data in the prototype is simulated. fNIRS and voice stress are marked as future work. Alert thresholds are project assumptions still to be calibrated. It is not a medical device.

Tools

Astro, TypeScript, SVG, anime.js, C for the bone and muscle algorithms.

Team 0G Health: Mikolaj Kurek, Abdelouahab Belarbi, Mamadou Ndiaye, Nourchene Jendoubi, Tresor Athawet, Suzon Gay.
